client: I've been really dreading this networking event that's coming up next week for work. Every time I think about walking into a room full of strangers and having to introduce myself and talk about what I do, my heart just starts racing and I feel kind of sick. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because when the moment actually comes, I'll still have to stand there and do it.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that your body is already reacting just from *thinking* about the event — that tells me how real and uncomfortable this feels for you, and I want you to know that's a very human response. You raise a fair point that talking alone won't make the moment disappear, and you're right — but what we *can* do together is gently loosen the grip that the dread has on you *before* you walk in, so it doesn't have to feel quite so overwhelming in that moment. 

I'm curious — when you imagine yourself standing in that room, what's the specific thought or fear that feels most loud or threatening to you?

client: When I imagine standing in that room, the loudest thought is probably something like... everyone's going to see that I don't belong there. Like they'll all somehow know that I've been struggling, that I'm barely holding it together, and they'll judge me for it. It's this fear that I'll be exposed, I guess, and that's when my chest gets really tight.
therapist:
That fear of being "exposed" is such a painful thing to carry into a room, and I really appreciate you naming it so clearly — that took courage. What's worth gently noticing is that this thought — *"everyone will see I don't belong"* — is a prediction your mind is making, not a fact that's already happened, and our minds often present those predictions with a lot more certainty than they deserve. 

I wonder, if you think back to other times you've been in social or professional situations while struggling internally, how often did people actually see through you in the way you're afraid of?

client: I mean... I guess if I'm being honest, most of the time people probably didn't notice. But that almost makes it worse somehow, like I was just performing the whole time and nobody knew, and I'm still performing now. It doesn't really make me feel less anxious about the next time, because I keep thinking eventually my luck will run out and someone will finally see it.
therapist: What you just described - that exhausting feeling of performing while hiding what's really going on inside - that's a really important thing to notice, and it sounds like the anxiety isn't just about *this* event but about a deeper fear of being truly known and found wanting. It's worth gently asking though: what exactly would it mean if someone *did* see that you've been struggling — is "being seen" as someone who's had a hard time actually the same thing as being unworthy of belonging there? What do you think that moment of "exposure" would actually reveal about you?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it logically, but emotionally it doesn't quite land that way. Like, I know struggling doesn't make me a bad person in theory, but when I imagine someone from my old program actually seeing that I've been barely holding it together since the career change... it just feels like proof that I made a mistake, that I don't really belong in this new field. It's less about being judged and more about confirming something I already fear about myself.
therapist:
What you just shared feels really significant — this isn't really about what *others* think at all, it's about a fear you're already carrying that the career change was a mistake, and you're worried this event might confirm that verdict you've already half-handed down on yourself. That's such a heavy thing to walk into a room with, and I want to sit with that for a moment rather than rush past it. 

I'm wondering — when you imagine the version of you who *does* belong in this new field, what would that person look like, and is it possible that someone in the middle of a hard transition could still genuinely be that person?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly, because when I picture someone who "belongs" in this field, I see someone confident, someone who doesn't second-guess every little decision, someone who just... knows things I feel like I'm still fumbling through. And then I think, okay, maybe I could get there eventually, but right now in the middle of all this uncertainty, it's really hard to believe that person and the person I am today are actually the same person on a continuum.
therapist:
The image you just described — confident, certain, never fumbling — that's a really worth examining, because I wonder if that person actually exists, or if they're a kind of impossible standard that even the most established people in your field are quietly measuring themselves against too. What's striking to me is that you *can* imagine a future version of yourself who belongs, which means some part of you hasn't fully closed the door on that possibility, even when it feels far away. 

What do you think it would mean for how you carry yourself at this event if "belonging" wasn't something you had to have already earned, but something that could coexist with still finding your footing?

client: That's... actually a kind of interesting way to put it, and I want to sit with it for a second because part of me wants to just dismiss it. Like, okay, sure, belonging can coexist with still finding my footing — that sounds nice in theory, but when I'm actually standing in that room and someone asks me about my work, the anxiety just takes over and I forget everything I know. I guess what I'm scared of is that "still finding my footing" will be written all over my face, and people will see right through me before I even get a chance to show what I can actually do.
therapist:
I really respect that you caught yourself wanting to dismiss it and chose to sit with it instead — that's actually a meaningful thing to notice. What you're describing in those anxious moments, where everything you know seems to vanish, is something we can genuinely work with practically before next week, because anxiety narrows our focus so sharply that it convinces us we're more transparent than we actually are — but that feeling of being "see-through" is mostly something happening *inside* you, not something broadcasting itself on your face. 

I'm curious — if you could go into that event with just one small, manageable intention rather than the pressure to prove you belong, what might that intention be?

client: I guess... maybe something like just trying to actually listen to one person instead of being stuck in my own head the whole time. But even saying that out loud, I'm already picturing myself at the event and feeling that tightness in my chest, like the intention just evaporates the second I walk through the door. It's hard to trust that something so small could actually hold up against how loud the anxiety gets in the moment.
therapist:
That intention — genuinely listening to one person — is actually beautifully chosen, because it shifts your focus *outward* onto them rather than inward onto how you're coming across, which is exactly what anxiety doesn't want you to do. Your skepticism about whether it will hold up is completely fair, and that's actually why it helps to practice connecting with that intention *now*, in moments like this when the anxiety is present but not at full volume, so it becomes a little more familiar and accessible when things get louder. 

What do you notice happening in your body right now, in this moment, as you imagine walking in with just that one small intention rather than the weight of having to prove yourself?

client: Honestly, when I imagine it that way, there's a tiny bit of loosening in my chest, like something unclenches just slightly. But then almost immediately my mind jumps in and says "yeah, but what if you forget that intention the second you walk through the door and the anxiety just takes over anyway." It's like I can feel the relief for a second and then my brain snatches it back.
therapist:
That tiny unclenching is really worth honoring, because your body just showed you something important — that a different relationship with this event is actually possible, even if your mind is quick to reclaim the worry. What you're describing, that snatching-back, is such a classic move anxiety makes, because it's threatened by that moment of relief and rushes in to close it down before it can take hold. 

What if we treated that flicker of loosening not as something fragile that has to survive the whole event, but as something you can actually return to — like a small anchor you've already found once and can find again?

client: I like the idea of it being an anchor, but I'm honestly not sure I'd be able to find it again in the moment when everything's ramping up. It's like, right now, sitting here talking about it, I can kind of feel that loosening again, but when I'm actually at the event and my heart's racing and I'm scanning the room feeling like nobody really wants me there... I don't know if I'd even remember to look for it. What if I reach for it and it's just not there?
therapist:
The fact that you've now felt that loosening *twice* in this conversation means it's not just a fluke — you're actually building a real, lived experience of it that your body is starting to recognize, and that's more than you had an hour ago. You're right that a racing heart and a scanning mind make it harder to reach for, which is exactly why it can help to pair that anchor with something physical and automatic — like a single slow exhale before you walk through the door — so your body has a way back to it even when your mind is loud.

What do you think it would feel like to give yourself permission, just for this one event, to treat that exhale and that intention to listen as "enough" — not a guarantee, but enough?

client: I think part of me wants to believe that could be enough, but there's this other part that immediately jumps in and says "what if it's not, though." Like, what if I do the exhale and set the intention and I still end up standing in the corner watching everyone else laugh and connect, and then I just feel worse because I tried and it still didn't work. That fear of trying and failing feels almost bigger than the fear of not trying at all.
therapist:
That fear of trying and failing is so understandable, because if you don't try, the story stays open — but if you try and it's hard, it can feel like evidence against yourself, and that's a really painful risk to take when you're already feeling fragile. But I want to gently reflect something back to you: standing in the corner after trying the exhale and the intention would actually mean you showed up, you reached for something, and you stayed — and that's a fundamentally different story than "I failed," even if it doesn't feel triumphant in the moment.

What do you think the version of you who made it through the evening — even imperfectly, even with some hard moments — would want you to know about what that actually took?
